Fat-tailed dwarf lemurs, Cheirogaleus medius, exhibit a fascinating reproductive strategy adapted to the seasonal environments of western Madagascar. Females typically produce a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], with litter sizes ranging from one to four pups [N_R_i = litter sizes ranging from one to four pups], an annual output that reflects the constraints of their hibernation-based life history. Data from captive colonies indicate that neonates have a wet weight at birth of just 19 grams [Wwb = 19 grams], a remarkably small size for a strepsirrhine primate that places the newborn completely dependent on maternal care. This altricial state is further underscored by the brief pre-weaning phase, as the time since birth at weaning is only 37 days [tx = 37 days], although this milestone is achieved only when maternal body temperature is maintained at a euthermic level of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. The short dependence period allows the mother to rapidly regain body condition before the onset of the dry season and her subsequent period of seasonal torpor.

Gestation in the fat-tailed dwarf lemur occupies a gestation time of 61 days [tg = 61 days] under normothermic conditions of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], a period that is relatively short compared to other lemurids of comparable size. This abbreviated gestation is likely an evolutionary response to the strict seasonal calendar imposed by Madagascar's unpredictable rainfall, which dictates the timing of resource availability for both the gestating female and her eventual offspring. Because the mother must accumulate sufficient fat reserves before entering hibernation, any delay in parturition could compromise her ability to survive the lean season. The 19 grams [Wwb = 19 grams] birth mass, while diminutive, is consistent with the species' overall pattern of producing small, rapidly developing offspring that transition to independence with exceptional speed. The prolonged maturation reflects the substantial energetic investment required to accumulate the fat stores needed for both hibernation and eventual reproduction. In contrast to many small-bodied mammals that reach sexual maturity within their birth year, the fat-tailed dwarf lemur's reliance on seasonal fattening imposes a life-history bottleneck that delays first reproduction until after the animal has survived its first full annual cycle of resource abundance and scarcity.

Maximum recorded longevity in this species, when corrected for the metabolic savings accrued during extended periods of seasonal torpor, reaches approximately 14.5 years [am = approximately 14.5 years] when measured under euthermic conditions of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This lifespan is exceptionally long for a mammal with an ultimate adult wet weight of only 380 grams [Wwi = 380 grams], as many rodents of similar size live only a few years in the wild. The extraordinary longevity of Cheirogaleus medius is directly attributable to its hibernation strategy, which dramatically reduces metabolic expenditure during the dry season. During torpor, body temperatures drop to near-ambient levels, and metabolic rates fall to a fraction of basal levels, effectively slowing the aging process. Consequently, the 380 grams [Wwi = 380 grams] asymptotic body mass is accumulated slowly over multiple active seasons, with individuals showing considerable plasticity in annual weight gain depending on local fruit abundance and the duration of the favorable wet season.

Adult body size in the fat-tailed dwarf lemur shows pronounced seasonal fluctuation, with individuals achieving their maximum wet weight of 380 grams [Wwi = 380 grams] just prior to entering hibernation, a critical threshold that determines overwinter survival. This seasonal mass gain is fueled by intense frugivory and gummivory during the wet season, during which individuals may double their lean body mass.
